blocks.x: When you open a terminal on Linux you are talking to a **shell** — a program that reads the commands you type, asks the kernel to run them, and shows you the result. The default shell on RHEL is **bash** (the Bourne-Again SHell). Everything you do on the RHCSA exam happens through this text interface, so being fast and confident here is the foundation for the whole exam. A command line usually has three parts: the **command** (the program to run), its **options** (flags that change how it behaves, like `-l`), and its **arguments** (what it acts on, like a filename). For example in `ls -l /etc`, `ls` is the command, `-l` is an option, and `/etc` is the argument.
Before every command the shell prints a **prompt**. On RHEL it looks like `[student@servera ~]$`. Read it carefully because it tells you a lot:
`student` is the user you are logged in as.
`servera` is the hostname of the machine.
`~` is your current directory (`~` means your home directory).
The final symbol is the most important: `$` means you are a **normal user**, while `#` means you are **root** (the all-powerful administrator). Always glance at this before running admin commands.
The exam has **no internet**, so knowing the built-in documentation is essential. Three sources cover almost everything:
**man pages** — `man command` opens the manual for a command. Inside, it uses the `less` pager: press Space to page down, `/word` to search, `n` for the next match, and `q` to quit.

**man sections** — the manual is split into numbered sections. Section 1 is user commands, section 5 is file formats (like `/etc/fstab`), and section 8 is admin commands. If a name exists in more than one section, pick the one you need: `man 5 passwd` shows the file format, `man 1 passwd` the command.
**`--help` and /usr/share/doc** — most commands accept `--help` for a quick summary, and installed packages drop examples and READMEs into `/usr/share/doc/<package>`.
If you do not know a command's name, search the descriptions with `man -k keyword` (also called `apropos`). If it says "nothing appropriate", build the index once as root with `mandb`.

1.h: Working faster with history and shortcuts

blocks.x: Bash remembers the commands you type. This saves huge amounts of time:
`history` lists past commands; `!42` reruns command number 42; `!!` reruns the previous command (handy as `sudo !!`); `!$` reuses the last argument of the previous command.
**Ctrl+R** starts a reverse search — type part of an old command and bash finds it; press Enter to run it.
**Tab completion** finishes filenames and command names for you; press Tab twice to see all matches.
`type name` tells you whether a name is a shell builtin, an alias, or a program on disk.

Linux organises everything under a single root directory called `/`. There are no drive letters like on Windows — even other disks appear as folders inside this one tree. The layout follows the **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)**, so the same directories mean the same thing on any RHEL system. Knowing where things live saves you from hunting during the exam:
`/etc` — system-wide **configuration** files.
`/home` — regular users' home directories; `/root` is root's home.
`/var` — **variable** data that changes as the system runs: logs in `/var/log`, spools, caches.
`/usr` — installed software (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/sbin`, libraries, `/usr/share/doc`).
`/boot` — the kernel and boot loader files.
`/tmp` — temporary files, wiped periodically.
`/dev` — device files; `/proc` and `/sys` — live kernel/hardware information.

A **path** is how you name a file's location. An **absolute path** starts from the root and always begins with `/`, for example `/home/student/notes.txt` — it works no matter where you currently are. A **relative path** is measured from your current directory, for example `notes.txt` or `../reports/q1.txt`. Two special names help you move around: `.` means "the current directory" and `..` means "the parent directory". `~` is a shortcut for your own home directory.
A few commands are your eyes and feet on the system:
`pwd` prints the directory you are standing in ("print working directory").
`cd` changes directory: `cd /etc` (absolute), `cd ..` (up one), `cd ~` or just `cd` (home), and `cd -` toggles back to the previous directory.

`ls` lists contents. The flags do the work: `-l` gives a detailed long listing, `-a` shows hidden dotfiles, `-h` shows human-readable sizes, `-t` sorts by time, `-R` recurses into subdirectories. You will use `ls -lah` constantly.
These verbs manage files and directories:
`mkdir` makes directories; `mkdir -p a/b/c` builds a whole nested path at once.
`touch file` creates an empty file (or updates a file's timestamp).
`cp source dest` copies; add `-r` to copy a whole directory tree, and `-a` (archive) to also preserve permissions, ownership and timestamps.
`mv` moves a file, or **renames** it if the target is in the same directory.

`rm` deletes files — there is **no recycle bin**, it is gone. `rm -r` removes a directory and everything in it, and `rm -f` forces with no prompt. `rm -rf` is powerful and dangerous, so double-check the path.

Two conveniences save typing: **brace expansion** like `touch file{1..5}.txt` creates file1 through file5, and **globbing** with wildcards where `*` matches any characters, `?` matches exactly one, and `[abc]` matches one character from a set.

3.h: Inodes: the real identity of a file

blocks.x: Every file on a Linux filesystem is really an **inode** — a numbered record holding the file's data location, permissions, owner, size and timestamps. The **name** you see in a directory is just a label that points to an inode. This idea explains how links work. See the inode number with `ls -i` or `stat`.

A **hard link** is an additional name pointing at the *same inode*. Both names are equal — neither is "the original" — and the file's data survives until the **last** name is removed. Because a hard link is just another directory entry for the same inode, it cannot cross to another filesystem and cannot point to a directory. The second column of `ls -l` shows the **link count**: how many names point to that inode. Create one with `ln target linkname` (no `-s`).

A **symbolic link** is different: it is a tiny special file that stores a *path* to another file, like a shortcut. Because it stores a path, it **can** cross filesystems and **can** point to directories — but if the target is deleted or moved, the link is left **dangling** (broken) and `ls -l` shows it in red. Create one with `ln -s target linkname`, and remember the order is always target first, then the link name.
`find` is the most powerful search tool because it walks the filesystem live and can test many properties and then act on the matches. The pattern is `find <where> <tests> <action>`:
Tests: `-name '*.conf'`, `-type f` (files) or `-type d` (directories), `-size +100M` (bigger than 100 MiB), `-mtime -1` (changed in the last day), `-user natasha`, `-perm -4000` (SUID bit set).
Action: by default it prints matches; `-ls` shows details; `-exec cmd {} \;` runs a command on each match, where `{}` becomes the matched path and `\;` ends the command.

A very common exam pattern is copying every file owned by a user: `find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/harry/ \; 2>/dev/null`. The `2>/dev/null` hides "Permission denied" errors from directories you cannot read. `locate name` is a faster name search using a prebuilt database, but the database can be stale — refresh it with `updatedb`.
Every Linux program automatically has three data streams, each with a number (a "file descriptor"):
**stdin** (0) — standard input, where the program reads from (normally the keyboard).
**stdout** (1) — standard output, where normal results go (normally the screen).
**stderr** (2) — standard error, where error messages go (also the screen by default, but a *separate* stream).
Keeping output and errors separate is what makes redirection powerful.
**Redirection** sends a stream to a file instead of the screen (or reads it from a file):
`command > file` sends stdout to a file, **overwriting** it. `command >> file` **appends** instead.
`command 2> file` sends only stderr to a file. `command 2>> file` appends errors.
`command > out 2>&1` sends stdout to `out`, then sends stderr to "wherever stdout now points" — so both go to `out`. Order matters here. The shorthand `command &> file` does the same.
`command < file` feeds a file into the program's stdin.
`/dev/null` is the "black hole": anything sent there is discarded, so `2>/dev/null` throws away errors.

A **pipe** `|` connects the **stdout** of one command to the **stdin** of the next, letting you build a chain where each tool does one job. For example `ls -l /etc | grep conf | wc -l` lists `/etc`, keeps only lines containing "conf", and counts them. Errors are not sent through a normal pipe unless you first merge them with `2>&1`.

4.h: tee: output to a file and the screen

blocks.x: Sometimes you want to *save* output and still *see* it. `tee` copies its input to a file **and** to stdout at the same time: `ls -l /etc | tee list.txt` shows the listing and writes it to `list.txt`. Use `tee -a` to append. A key exam habit: only produce exactly what a task asks for — do not add `sort` or other changes unless the task says so, because the grader checks the actual file.

5.h: Reading files without opening an editor

blocks.x: Often you just want to *look* at a file:
`cat file` dumps the whole file to the screen (and can join files: `cat a b > c`).
`less file` shows it one screen at a time — Space pages down, `b` pages back, `/word` searches, `q` quits. It is the same pager `man` uses.

`head file` shows the first 10 lines (`head -n 20` for 20); `tail` shows the last 10. **`tail -f file` follows a file live** as new lines are added — essential for watching logs such as `tail -f /var/log/secure`.

`echo` prints text or the value of a variable: `echo "Hello"`, `echo $PATH`. Combined with redirection it is a quick way to create or append to files: `echo "a line" >> notes.txt`. Variables in bash are written `$NAME`; double quotes `"$NAME"` expand the variable while keeping spaces intact, whereas single quotes `'$NAME'` treat it literally.
`nano` is a beginner-friendly terminal editor. The important shortcuts are shown at the bottom of the screen: **Ctrl+O** writes (saves) the file, **Ctrl+X** exits. It is fine for quick edits.
`vim` is the editor to know for the exam because it is always installed. It is **modal**, meaning keys do different things depending on the mode:

**Normal (command) mode** is where you start — keys move and edit. `dd` cuts a line, `yy` copies a line, `p` pastes, `u` undoes, `Ctrl+R` redoes, `gg` jumps to the top, `G` to the bottom, `:set nu` shows line numbers.
**Insert mode** is for typing text — press `i` to insert before the cursor, `a` to append after it, or `o` to open a new line below. Press **Esc** to return to normal mode.
**Command-line mode** starts with `:` — `:w` writes, `:q` quits, `:wq` (or `ZZ`) writes and quits, `:q!` quits without saving, and `:%s/old/new/g` replaces every "old" with "new" in the whole file.
If you only learn one thing: press **Esc**, then type `:wq` to save and quit, or `:q!` to bail out. Running `vimtutor` once (about 30 minutes) teaches everything you need.

`grep` searches text for lines matching a pattern and prints those lines. It is the workhorse of log analysis and config inspection. The basic form is `grep pattern file`, and it also reads from a pipe: `command | grep pattern`. Useful options:

`-i` ignores case, `-v` inverts the match (lines that do **not** match), `-c` counts matching lines, `-n` shows line numbers, `-w` matches whole words only, `-r` searches recursively through a directory, and `-l` prints only the names of matching files.
A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern language that makes grep powerful. The core pieces:
`^` anchors to the **start** of a line, `$` anchors to the **end**. So `^root` matches lines starting with root, and `bash$` matches lines ending with bash. `^$` matches an empty line.
`.` matches any single character; escape it as `\.` to mean a literal dot.
`*` means "zero or more of the previous item".

With **extended** regex (`grep -E`), you also get `|` (or), `+` (one or more), `?` (optional), and `{n}` (repeat) without needing backslashes. For example `grep -E 'cat|dog'` matches lines containing cat or dog.
A few patterns come up again and again:
Show what a config file really sets, ignoring comments and blank lines: `grep -Ev '^#|^$' /etc/ssh/sshd_config`.
List the users who use the bash shell from `/etc/passwd`: `grep '/bin/bash$' /etc/passwd`.
Count failed SSH logins in the security log: `grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/secure`.
Combine grep with `cut -d: -f1` to keep just the first colon-separated field (like the username in `/etc/passwd`).

7.h: Users, UIDs and the account files

blocks.x: Every person or service on the system is a **user account** identified by a number called a **UID**. Three files define accounts:
`/etc/passwd` holds one line per user with seven colon-separated fields: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The password field is just `x` because the real hash lives elsewhere.
`/etc/shadow` holds the encrypted password hashes and password-aging information; it is readable only by root.
`/etc/group` defines groups.
On RHEL, **root** is UID 0, system accounts use UIDs 1–999, and the first regular user gets UID **1000** (the range comes from `/etc/login.defs`).

7.h: Groups and the user private group scheme

blocks.x: A **group** lets you give a set of users the same access. Each user has one **primary group** (used for files they create) and any number of **supplementary groups**. RHEL uses the **user private group** scheme: creating user `harry` also creates a group called `harry` as his primary group. This keeps each user's files private by default while still allowing shared groups for teamwork.
The core commands:
`useradd harry` creates a user (with `-u` to set the UID, `-s` to set the login shell, `-G` to add supplementary groups, `-c` for a comment/full name).
`passwd harry` sets or changes a password; `echo 'secret' | passwd --stdin harry` sets it non-interactively (handy in scripts and the exam).

`usermod` changes an existing account. The most important rule: to **add** a supplementary group without wiping the others, always use `usermod -aG groupname user` — the `-a` means "append". Leaving out `-a` **replaces** the whole supplementary list.
`userdel -r harry` deletes the account **and** its home directory; without `-r` the home directory is left behind.
`groupadd`, `groupmod` and `groupdel` manage groups; `id harry` and `getent passwd harry` show what an account looks like.
A shell of `/sbin/nologin` gives an account that cannot log in interactively — used for service accounts.

8.h: Why passwords live in two files

blocks.x: When you log in, Linux checks your password. But the account details and the secret password are kept apart for safety. `/etc/passwd` is readable by everyone and holds the account basics; the actual scrambled password (a **hash**) lives in `/etc/shadow`, which only root can read. This way an ordinary user can look up account info without ever seeing the hashes.
`passwd` changes a password.
As a normal user, typing `passwd` on its own changes **your own** password (it asks for the current one first).
As **root**, `passwd harry` sets another user's password without knowing the old one.
`echo 'Secret123' | passwd --stdin harry` (RHEL-only) sets a password without the interactive prompt — very useful in scripts and on the exam.

`passwd -l harry` **locks** an account (puts a `!` in front of the hash so no password works); `passwd -u harry` unlocks it; `passwd -e harry` **expires** the password so the user must change it at next login.
"Aging" means forcing passwords to change over time. `chage` (change age) controls this per user:
`chage -l harry` **lists** harry's current aging settings in plain language — always start here.
`chage -M 90 harry` sets the **maximum** days a password is valid (must change every 90 days).
`chage -m 7 harry` sets the **minimum** days before it can be changed again.
`chage -W 7 harry` sets the **warning** days before expiry.
`chage -E 2026-12-31 harry` sets an **account** expiry date (the whole account stops working after that day).
`chage -d 0 harry` sets the last-change date to zero, which counts as already expired — so harry must set a new password at next login.

System-wide defaults for **new** users live in `/etc/login.defs` (look for `PASS_MAX_DAYS`, `PASS_MIN_DAYS`, `PASS_WARN_AGE`). Changing that file only affects accounts created afterward; existing users need `chage`.

8.h: Becoming another user: su and sudo

blocks.x: Sometimes you need more power than your own account has.

`su - harry` **switches** to harry (asks for harry's password). The dash is important: `su -` starts a full **login shell**, loading harry's environment and moving to his home directory. Without the dash you keep your own environment. `su -` with no name means "become root".

`sudo command` runs a single command **as root** (or another user), but you type **your own** password, and only if you have been granted permission. This is safer than sharing the root password and it logs who did what.
On RHEL, members of the **wheel** group get full sudo by default. Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel harry`.
sudo's rules live in `/etc/sudoers`, but you must **never** edit it directly with a plain editor — a typo can lock everyone out. Instead:
Run `visudo`, which checks the syntax before saving.
Better, drop a small file into `/etc/sudoers.d/` (e.g. `/etc/sudoers.d/admins`) and check it with `visudo -c`.

A rule looks like `harry ALL=(ALL) ALL` (harry may run any command as anyone). A group rule starts with `%`: `%sysmgrs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` lets the sysmgrs group run anything as root **without** a password. `%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL` is the default wheel rule.

Linux is multi-user, so every file and directory records **who may do what** with it. Look at the left of `ls -l` output, for example `-rwxr-xr--`. That is ten characters: the first is the **type** (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` link), and the remaining nine are three groups of three permissions.

9.h: The three who's and the three what's

blocks.x: Permissions are set for three classes of people:
**u** = the **user** who owns the file (owner).
**g** = the **group** that owns the file.
**o** = **others** (everyone else).
And three kinds of access:
**r** (read) = 4, **w** (write) = 2, **x** (execute) = 1.
So `rwxr-xr--` means: owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, others can only read.

9.h: What r, w, x mean on directories (the tricky part)

blocks.x: On a **file** the meanings are obvious. On a **directory** they are different:
**r** lets you **list** the names inside (e.g. run `ls`).
**x** lets you **enter** the directory and reach files inside (traverse it). Without `x` you cannot `cd` in, even if you can read the name list.
**w** (plus x) lets you **create and delete** entries inside.
A common bug: a file is readable but a user still cannot open it — usually because a parent directory is missing `x` for them. Trace the whole path with `namei -l /path/to/file`.
`chmod` changes permissions two ways.

**Symbolic mode** spells out who/operator/what: `chmod g+w file` adds write for group, `chmod o-rwx file` removes all from others, `chmod u=rwx,go=rx file` sets exact values, and `chmod a+x file` adds execute for all (a = all three classes).

**Octal (numeric) mode** adds up r=4, w=2, x=1 for each class: `chmod 755 file` = rwx (7) for owner, r-x (5) for group, r-x (5) for others. `chmod 644` is the normal file default (rw-r--r--), `chmod 600` is owner-only. `chmod -R` applies changes recursively through a directory tree.
`chown harry file` changes the **owner** to harry (root only).
`chown harry:sysmgrs file` changes owner **and** group at once.
`chown :sysmgrs file` changes just the group (same as `chgrp sysmgrs file`).
`chown -R harry:sysmgrs /data` changes ownership through a whole tree.
A regular owner may change a file's group only to a group they belong to; only root can give a file to a different user.
Beyond rwx there are three **special bits** that change behaviour, shown in place of an `x` in `ls -l`:

**SUID** (Set User ID, value 4) on an executable makes it run with the **owner's** privileges instead of yours. That is how `passwd` (owned by root) can update `/etc/shadow` when you run it. Shown as an `s` in the owner's execute slot (`-rwsr-xr-x`).
**SGID** (Set Group ID, value 2) on a **directory** makes new files inside inherit the directory's **group** — perfect for shared team folders. Shown as `s` in the group slot.
**Sticky bit** (value 1) on a directory means users can only **delete their own** files there, even if the directory is world-writable. `/tmp` uses it, shown as `t` in the others slot (`drwxrwxrwt`).
Set them in octal by prefixing a fourth digit: `chmod 2770 dir` (SGID), `chmod 1777 dir` (sticky), `chmod 4755 file` (SUID). Or symbolically: `chmod g+s dir`, `chmod +t dir`, `chmod u+s file`.

10.h: umask: the default for new files

blocks.x: When you create a file, its starting permissions are decided by the **umask**, which *removes* bits from a base. New files start from 666 and new directories from 777, then the umask is subtracted.
With `umask 022`, files become 644 (666−022) and directories 755 — the common default.
With `umask 077`, files become 600 and directories 700 — private to you.
Run `umask` alone to see the current value. To make a umask permanent for one user, add the `umask` line to their `~/.bashrc`; for everyone, put a script in `/etc/profile.d/`.

10.h: Access Control Lists (ACLs) for finer control

blocks.x: Standard permissions only cover one owner, one group, and others. **ACLs** let you grant a *specific* extra user or group their own permissions on a file.
`getfacl file` shows the ACL.
`setfacl -m u:natasha:rw file` gives user natasha read+write. `setfacl -m g:auditors:r file` grants a group.
`setfacl -m u:harry:--- file` gives harry no access at all (a named-user entry beats the "others" bits).
`setfacl -x u:natasha file` removes one entry; `setfacl -b file` removes all ACL entries.
On a directory, a **default** ACL applies to files created later: `setfacl -m d:u:harry:rwx dir`.
A file that has an ACL shows a `+` at the end of its `ls -l` permission string (e.g. `-rw-r--r--+`).

A running program is a **process**. Each has a unique number, the **PID** (Process ID), and belongs to a user. The kernel schedules processes onto the CPU. Understanding how to see, prioritise and stop processes is core system administration.

11.h: Seeing what is running: ps and top

blocks.x: `ps` shows a snapshot of processes. The most common form is `ps aux` (every process, with user and resource use). `ps -ef` is another full listing. Add sorting: `ps aux --sort=-%cpu` (biggest CPU first) or `--sort=-%mem` (biggest memory).
`top` (or the friendlier `htop`) is a **live** view that refreshes every few seconds. Inside top: press **P** to sort by CPU, **M** by memory, **k** to kill a PID, **r** to renice, and **q** to quit.
Process **states** you will see: R (running), S (sleeping), T (stopped), Z (zombie), D (uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on disk).
You control processes by sending them **signals** (messages).
`kill PID` sends **SIGTERM (15)** by default — a polite "please exit cleanly".
`kill -9 PID` sends **SIGKILL (9)** — force-quit, which a process cannot catch or ignore. Use it only when SIGTERM does not work.
Other useful signals: **SIGHUP (1)** often tells a daemon to reload; **SIGSTOP** pauses a process and **SIGCONT** resumes it.
`pkill name` and `killall name` kill by **name** instead of PID; `pgrep name` lists matching PIDs first so you can check before killing. `pkill -u harry` targets all of a user's processes.
A command normally runs in the **foreground**, holding your terminal. You can move work to the **background**:
Add `&` to start a command in the background: `sleep 1000 &`.
Press **Ctrl+Z** to **suspend** (pause) the foreground job; **Ctrl+C** sends SIGINT to end it.
`jobs` lists background jobs; `bg %1` resumes job 1 in the background; `fg %1` brings it to the foreground.
`nohup command &` runs something immune to hang-ups so it keeps running after you log out.
Every process has a **nice value** from **−20** (highest priority, greediest) to **19** (lowest, most generous to others); the default is 0.
`nice -n 10 command` starts a command with a nicer (lower) priority.
`renice -n 5 -p 1234` changes the priority of running PID 1234.
Only **root** can *raise* priority (give a more negative nice); regular users can only make their own processes nicer.

On modern RHEL, **systemd** is the first process to start (PID 1) and it manages everything else. The things it manages are called **units**. The most common unit type is a **service** (a background program, or "daemon"), whose files end in `.service`. Other unit types include targets, sockets, and timers.

12.h: systemctl: the one command to know

blocks.x: `systemctl` controls units. The verbs are intuitive:
`systemctl status sshd` — show whether it is running, plus recent log lines.
`systemctl start sshd` / `stop sshd` / `restart sshd` — control it **now**.
`systemctl reload sshd` — tell it to re-read its config **without** stopping (not all services support it; `reload-or-restart` covers both).
`systemctl enable sshd` — make it start **at boot**; `disable` undoes that. These do **not** affect the current run — that is why `enable --now sshd` (enable *and* start) is so handy.
`systemctl is-active sshd` and `is-enabled sshd` answer the two separate questions: running now? starting at boot?

12.h: Enabled vs active — two different things

blocks.x: This trips up beginners: **enabled** is about the *next boot*, **active** is about *right now*. A service can be enabled but stopped, or running but not enabled. The exam usually wants services that are **both** running and enabled — so `systemctl enable --now name` is your go-to.
`systemctl mask atd` links a unit to `/dev/null` so it **cannot** be started at all, even manually — a strong "off switch". `systemctl unmask atd` reverses it.
`systemctl list-units --type=service` lists running services; `list-unit-files` shows every installed unit and its boot state; `--failed` shows what has failed.

`systemctl cat sshd` prints a unit's file; `systemctl daemon-reload` makes systemd re-read unit files after you add or edit one (files you write go in `/etc/systemd/system/`, which overrides the packaged copies in `/usr/lib/systemd/system/`).

**SSH** (Secure Shell) lets you log in to and run commands on another machine over an **encrypted** connection. It replaced old plaintext tools like Telnet, which sent passwords in the clear. The client command is `ssh`; the server is the `sshd` service listening on TCP port **22**.
`ssh student@servera` opens an interactive shell on servera as student.
`ssh student@servera hostname` runs a single command remotely and returns just its output.

The first time you connect, SSH shows the server's **host key fingerprint** and asks you to accept it; it is then stored in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If a host is reinstalled its key changes and you will be warned — remove the stale entry with `ssh-keygen -R servera`.
Copy files over SSH with `scp file user@host:/path` (or `scp user@host:/path localfile` to pull), and `sftp user@host` for an interactive file transfer session.
Instead of typing a password every time, you can use a **key pair**: a private key you keep secret and a matching public key you place on the server.
`ssh-keygen` creates the pair in `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`/`id_ed25519` private, `.pub` public). Press Enter for defaults; you may add a passphrase for extra safety.
`ssh-copy-id student@servera` copies your public key into the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` and fixes the permissions automatically.
After that, `ssh student@servera` logs in using the key, no password needed.
Permissions matter: the server ignores your key unless `~/.ssh` is `700` and `authorized_keys` is `600` (this is "StrictModes").
The server's config is `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (and drop-in files in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`). Two important settings:
`PermitRootLogin no` stops root logging in directly over SSH.
`PasswordAuthentication no` forces key-only login (set up your key **first**, or you will lock yourself out).
Always check the syntax with `sshd -t` before applying, then `systemctl reload sshd`. Note `/etc/ssh/ssh_config` is the **client** config — don't confuse it with the server's `sshd_config`.

RHEL records events in two ways. The **systemd journal** (managed by `systemd-journald`) is a structured, queryable log of everything systemd and its services produce. Alongside it, **rsyslog** writes traditional plain-text log files under `/var/log/`. Key files: `/var/log/messages` (general system messages) and `/var/log/secure` (authentication and security events like SSH logins).
`journalctl` queries the journal. Learn these filters:
`journalctl` alone shows everything (in the `less` pager); `-n 20` shows the last 20 lines; `-f` **follows** live like `tail -f`.
`journalctl -u sshd` limits output to one **unit** (service). Combine with `-f` to watch a service live.
`journalctl -p err` filters by **priority** (err and worse). Priorities from most to least severe: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug (numbered 0–7).
`journalctl -b` shows only the **current boot**; `-b -1` the previous boot; `--list-boots` lists them.
`journalctl --since "1 hour ago"` or `--since "2026-10-01 09:00" --until "10:00"` limits by time.
`journalctl _UID=1000` or `_COMM=sshd` filter by fields; `-o verbose` shows one entry in full detail.
By default (`Storage=auto`) the journal is kept in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is **lost on reboot** unless a directory exists to persist it. To keep it:
Create `/var/log/journal` (or set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`), then restart `systemd-journald`.
After a reboot, `journalctl --list-boots` should show more than one boot, proving persistence works.

`logger` writes a message into the log system, useful for testing rules and scripts: `logger -p user.notice "hello"`. Check it landed with `journalctl -n 5` or `tail /var/log/messages`. rsyslog's routing rules live in `/etc/rsyslog.conf` and drop-in files in `/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf`; a rule like `authpriv.*  /var/log/secure` means "all authpriv-facility messages go to that file".

A correct, synchronised clock is more important than beginners expect. Log timestamps, scheduled jobs, TLS certificates and cluster software all depend on accurate time. If two machines disagree on the time, investigating an incident by comparing their logs becomes almost impossible. RHEL keeps time in sync over the network using **NTP** (Network Time Protocol), implemented by the **chrony** service (`chronyd`).

15.h: timedatectl: the clock and time zone

blocks.x: `timedatectl` is the single command for date, time and time zone:
`timedatectl` (or `timedatectl status`) shows the current time, the time zone, and whether NTP sync is active. Look for "System clock synchronized: yes".
`timedatectl list-timezones` lists all zone names; pipe to `grep Asia` to narrow it.
`timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Kolkata` sets the zone (this updates the `/etc/localtime` link).
`timedatectl set-ntp true` turns network time sync on (enabling and starting chronyd); `set-ntp false` turns it off.
`timedatectl set-time "2026-12-25 10:00:00"` sets the clock manually (only works with NTP off).
chrony's config is `/etc/chrony.conf`. The important line names a time source:
`server classroom.example.com iburst` syncs from one specific server; `iburst` speeds up the first sync.
`pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst` uses a pool name that resolves to many servers.
After editing, apply with `systemctl restart chronyd` (and `enable` it for boot). To make a machine an NTP **server** for your LAN, add `allow 192.168.122.0/24`.

`chronyc sources` lists the time sources chrony is using. In the output, `^*` marks the server it is currently synced to, and `^?` means "not reachable yet" (wait a minute after a restart). Add `-v` for a legend.
`chronyc tracking` shows how accurate the local clock is and its offset from the reference.

On RHEL, the network is controlled by **NetworkManager**, and you configure it with the `nmcli` command. NetworkManager stores each network setup as a **connection profile** (a saved configuration), separate from the physical **device** (the network card, like `eth0`). One device can have several profiles; you activate whichever one you need.

16.h: IP addresses, netmasks and gateways (the basics)

blocks.x: An **IP address** identifies a machine on a network, e.g. `192.168.122.11`.
A **netmask** (written as a prefix like `/24`) says how much of the address is the network part. `/24` equals `255.255.255.0`.
The **gateway** is the router the machine sends traffic to when the destination is on another network.
A **DNS server** turns names (like `servera`) into IP addresses.

16.h: Viewing the network with ip and nmcli

blocks.x: `ip a` (short for `ip addr`) shows every interface and its addresses; `ip -br a` gives one tidy line each. `ip route` shows the routing table, including the `default via …` gateway line.
`nmcli con show` lists connection profiles; add `--active` to see which are live. `nmcli device status` shows devices and which profile each uses.

16.h: Setting a static IP with nmcli

blocks.x: The pattern is to **modify** a profile, then **bring it up**:

`nmcli con mod "profile" ipv4.addresses 192.168.122.11/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.122.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.122.1 ipv4.method manual` sets a static configuration. `ipv4.method manual` is essential — without it the profile may keep using DHCP.

`nmcli con up "profile"` re-activates the profile so the changes take effect (they do **not** apply until you do this — and if you are connected over SSH, changing the IP will drop your session, so use the console).
Use `+ipv4.addresses` to add a second address without removing the first.
Profiles are stored as keyfiles in `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/`.
`hostnamectl set-hostname server1.example.com` sets the machine's name permanently (writing `/etc/hostname`).

`/etc/hosts` is a simple local file mapping IP addresses to names; it is checked **before** DNS. Add a line like `192.168.122.12 server2` to reach a host by name without a DNS server. `getent hosts server2` shows what the system actually resolves.

The internet is running out of the older **IPv4** addresses (the `192.168.x.x` style), so **IPv6** was created with vastly more addresses, written in hex groups like `fd00:10::11`. You configure it almost the same way as IPv4:
`nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::11/64 ipv6.method manual` then `nmcli con up eth0`.
The IPv6 loopback (this machine) is `::1`, the IPv4 equivalent of `127.0.0.1`.
Addresses starting `fe80::` are **link-local** — created automatically on every interface and only valid on the local link. Your real routable address shows as "scope global" in `ip a`.
DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names to IP addresses. Useful lookup tools:
`dig servera.example.com` gives detailed DNS answers; `dig servera +short` gives just the address. `dig example.com MX` looks up mail servers, `NS` name servers, `TXT` text records.
`host servera` is a simpler resolver; `nslookup` is another.
`getent hosts servera` resolves a name the way real applications do — using the full order in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (usually files, then DNS) — so it reflects `/etc/hosts` **and** DNS.
The DNS servers the system uses appear in `/etc/resolv.conf`, but on RHEL you set them through NetworkManager (`ipv4.dns`), not by editing that file directly.

17.h: A calm way to troubleshoot connectivity

blocks.x: When something "can't connect", work up the stack in order instead of guessing:
**Link** — is the interface up with an IP? `ip -br a`, `ip -br link`.
**Route** — is there a default gateway? `ip route`.
**Gateway** — can you reach it? `ping -c2 <gateway>`.
**DNS** — does the name resolve? `getent hosts <name>` or `dig <name>`.
**Service** — is the remote port open? `ss -tulpn` locally, or `nc -zv host 443` to a remote port.
`ss -tulpn` is the modern replacement for `netstat`: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric ports.

Instead of copying files around, Linux installs software as **packages**. On RHEL these are **RPM** packages (`.rpm` files). Each package bundles the program plus information about what other packages it needs (its **dependencies**). Two tools work with them: the low-level `rpm` (queries and installs a single file) and the high-level `dnf` (resolves dependencies and downloads from repositories).
`rpm` is best for asking questions about **already-installed** packages (the `-q` = query flag):
`rpm -qa` lists all installed packages (pipe to `grep` to search).
`rpm -qf /etc/ssh/sshd_config` says which package **owns** a given file.
`rpm -ql openssh-server` lists all files a package installed; `-qc` shows just its config files; `-qd` its documentation; `-qi` general info.
`rpm -qip file.rpm` and `-qlp file.rpm` query a `.rpm` **file** that is not installed yet (the `p` = package file).
`dnf` is what you use day to day because it handles dependencies and repositories:

`dnf install httpd` downloads httpd **and** anything it needs. `dnf install ./local.rpm` installs a local file but still pulls dependencies from repos (better than `rpm -ivh`, which just fails if something is missing).
`dnf remove httpd` uninstalls it (and packages that depend on it — read the list before confirming).
`dnf update` updates everything; `dnf search word` and `dnf provides */semanage` find packages (the second finds which package provides a command).
`dnf list installed`, `dnf info httpd`, and package **groups** via `dnf group list` / `dnf group install "Development Tools"`.
`dnf history` lists past transactions; `dnf history info last` details one; `dnf history undo last` reverses it.

Kernels are special "install-only" packages: a `dnf update` **adds** the new kernel alongside the old ones (used after a reboot) so you can still boot an older, working kernel from the GRUB menu if a new one misbehaves.

A **repository** (repo) is a collection of packages that `dnf` can download from, plus an index of what's available. Without a repo, `dnf` has nowhere to fetch software. On the RHCSA exam you often have to point a machine at a repo yourself.
Repo definitions are `.repo` files in `/etc/yum.repos.d/`. A minimal working repo section needs just a few lines:
`[myrepo]` — a short id in square brackets.
`name=My Repo` — a human name.
`baseurl=…` — where the packages are. This can be `http://host/path`, or a local path as `file:///mnt/iso/BaseOS` (three slashes: `file://` + the absolute path).
`enabled=1` — turn it on.
`gpgcheck=0` (or `1` with a `gpgkey=` line) — whether to verify signatures.

You can also add one with `dnf config-manager --add-repo <url>`, and enable/disable with `dnf config-manager --set-enabled`/`--set-disabled`. Check your work with `dnf repolist` (add `all` to include disabled ones), then install a package to prove it works.

19.h: Flatpak: a different kind of package

blocks.x: **Flatpak** is a newer, cross-distribution way to install desktop **applications**, sandboxed and independent of the system packages. It uses **remotes** (its version of repositories):
`flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo` adds the popular Flathub remote.
`flatpak remotes` lists configured remotes; `flatpak remote-ls flathub` lists apps a remote offers.

`flatpak install flathub org.gnome.Calculator` installs an app system-wide (add `--user` to install only for you); `flatpak list` shows what is installed; `flatpak run <app-id>` starts one; `flatpak uninstall <app-id>` removes it.

Bundling many files into one **archive** makes them easy to move or back up, and **compression** makes that bundle smaller. On Linux the classic tool is `tar` (tape archive), which can also compress by calling gzip, bzip2 or xz.
tar's letters combine, and beginners find them clearer once named:
**c** = create, **x** = extract, **t** = list (test contents), **f** = the archive **f**ilename (always needed), **v** = verbose (show files as they are processed).
Compression: **z** = gzip (`.tar.gz`), **j** = bzip2 (`.tar.bz2`), **J** = xz (`.tar.xz`).

So `tar -czf /root/etc.tar.gz /etc` **c**reates a g**z**ipped archive **f**ile of `/etc`. `tar -xzf etc.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore` e**x**tracts it into a chosen directory (`-C` = change to that directory first). `tar -tzf etc.tar.gz` **lists** contents without extracting. Modern tar auto-detects compression on extract, so `z/j/J` is optional when reading. When tar prints "Removing leading '/'", it is storing paths **relative** so extracting never overwrites the originals by accident — they land under your current (or `-C`) directory.
`gzip file` compresses `file` into `file.gz` (replacing the original); `gunzip file.gz` reverses it. `gzip -k` keeps the original.
`zip -r archive.zip folder` and `unzip archive.zip` handle the cross-platform ZIP format.
`scp file user@host:/path` copies over SSH (encrypted). Add `-r` for directories. Reverse the arguments to pull: `scp user@host:/path localfile`.
`sftp user@host` opens an interactive session (`get`, `put`, `ls`, `bye`).

`rsync -av source/ user@host:/dest/` efficiently syncs directories, copying only what changed. A **trailing slash** on the source means "the contents of source" go into dest, rather than the source folder itself — a classic gotcha.

Disks appear under `/dev` with names like `/dev/vda` (a whole disk) and `/dev/vda1` (a partition on it). A **filesystem** (like XFS or ext4) is the structure that lets a partition hold files. To use a filesystem you **mount** it onto an empty directory (the **mount point**); everything under that directory then lives on that filesystem.
`lsblk` lists block devices as a tree (disks, partitions, sizes, mount points); `lsblk -f` adds filesystem type and **UUID**.
`df -h` shows free space on mounted filesystems in human-readable units; `df -hT` adds the type. Remember: `df` reports **filesystems**.
`du -sh /var/log` shows how much space files **use** (`-s` summary, `-h` human); `du -h --max-depth=1 /var` breaks it down by subdirectory.
`blkid` prints each filesystem's UUID and type — the UUID is a stable id you use in `/etc/fstab` because device names (`/dev/vdb1`) can change between boots.
`mount /dev/vdb1 /mnt/data` attaches a filesystem for now (the mount point directory must already exist).

`umount /mnt/data` detaches it. If it says "target is busy", something is using it — often your own shell sitting inside it. `cd` out, then find other users with `lsof /mnt/data` or `fuser -vm /mnt/data`.
`findmnt /mnt/data` confirms what is mounted where.
Permanent mounts belong in `/etc/fstab` (covered in the storage days) using `UUID=` or `LABEL=` so they survive reboots.

21.h: Logging in on text consoles and switching users

blocks.x: When there is no desktop, RHEL provides several text **consoles**. Switch between them with **Ctrl+Alt+F2** through **F6** (in a VM, send the keys from the VM window's menu). To see who is around and become another user:
`who` and `w` show who is logged in (`w` also shows what each person is running); `last` shows past logins.
`su - harry` becomes harry (needs harry's password); `sudo -i` gives a root login shell using **your** password (if you have sudo rights). Type `exit` to return to your own account.

A **shell script** is just a text file containing the same commands you would type in the terminal, saved so you can run them again as one command. Instead of typing ten steps every time, you put them in a file and run the file. This is how administrators automate repetitive work.

22.h: The shebang and making a script runnable

blocks.x: The first line of a script should be the **shebang**: `#!/bin/bash`. The `#!` tells the kernel which interpreter (here bash) should run the file. Without it, the system may not know how to execute your script. A fresh text file is not executable, so you must give it the execute permission:
`chmod +x script.sh` makes it runnable.
Run it with `./script.sh` (the `./` means "in the current directory"), or put it in a directory on your PATH like `/usr/local/bin/` so you can call it by name from anywhere.

A **variable** stores a value. Assign with no spaces around the `=`: `name="Purva"` (writing `name = "Purva"` fails because bash thinks `name` is a command). Read it back with a `$`: `echo "$name"`. Always quote variables in double quotes so spaces stay intact. **Command substitution** captures the output of a command into a variable: `today=$(date +%F)` stores today's date. The `$( )` form is preferred over the older backticks.
When you run `./greet.sh Purva`, the script receives that word as an input:
`$1`, `$2`, `$3` … are the first, second, third arguments.
`$0` is the script's own name.
`$#` is the **number** of arguments given.
`$@` is **all** the arguments (quote it as `"$@"` to keep each intact).
This lets one script behave differently depending on what you pass it.

Every command returns an **exit status**: `0` means success, any other number means failure. The special variable `$?` holds the status of the **last** command, so you can test whether it worked. In your own scripts, `exit 0` ends with success and `exit 1` (or any non-zero) signals an error. Send error messages to standard error with `>&2` by convention.

Scripts become useful when they can **decide**. The `if` statement runs code only when a test is true: ``` if [ "$x" = "yes" ]; then echo ok else echo no fi ``` The spaces inside `[ ]` are required, and the block ends with `fi` (if spelled backwards). `[ ]` is actually the `test` command in disguise.
Tests come in two flavours:

**Numbers**: `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-lt` (less than), `-le`, `-gt` (greater than), `-ge`. Example: `[ "$n" -gt 5 ]`. Note that inside `[ ]`, the symbol `>` means redirection, not comparison — so use `-gt`.
**Strings**: `=` and `!=`. `[ -z "$s" ]` is true when the string is empty; `[ -n "$s" ]` when it is not.
**Files**: `-f file` (a regular file exists), `-d dir` (a directory), `-e` (exists, any type), `-r`/`-w`/`-x` (readable/writable/executable), `-s` (not empty).

A **loop** repeats work. The `for` loop steps through a list: ``` for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done ``` The list can be numbers (`{1..5}`), files (`for f in /etc/*.conf`), or command output. A `while` loop repeats **as long as** a condition is true — the classic pattern reads a file line by line: ``` while read line; do echo "$line"; done < users.txt ``` This safely handles each line even if it contains spaces.

`&&` runs the next command only if the previous **succeeded**; `||` runs it only if the previous **failed** — e.g. `[ -r /etc/hosts ] && echo yes`. For choosing between many fixed values, `case` is cleaner than a chain of ifs, and each branch ends with `;;`, with the whole block closed by `esac`.
Sometimes a task should run **later** or **repeatedly** without you being there. RHEL offers two classic tools:
**at** runs a command **once** at a future time.
**cron** runs commands **repeatedly** on a schedule.
(A third, modern option — systemd timers — is covered on the next day.)

24.h: Scheduling a one-off job with at

blocks.x: `at` reads the command from standard input and runs it once:
`echo "command" | at now + 5 minutes` schedules it 5 minutes from now. Other time forms: `at 16:30`, `at 9am tomorrow`, `at noon + 2 days`.
`atq` (or `at -l`) lists pending jobs; `at -c 3` shows the full script of job 3; `atrm 3` (or `at -d 3`) deletes it.
The `atd` service must be running for jobs to fire.

Each user has a **crontab** (cron table). Edit yours with `crontab -e`; list it with `crontab -l`; remove it with `crontab -r`. As root you can manage another user's with `-u`: `crontab -e -u natasha`. A crontab line has **five time fields** then the command: ``` minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week   command ```

`*` means "every". `30 14 * * *` = 14:30 every day. `*/10 * * * *` = every 10 minutes. `0 2 * * 0` = 02:00 every Sunday (0 or 7 = Sunday). `30 23 1,15 * *` = 23:30 on the 1st and 15th (commas list values, dashes give ranges).

Besides per-user crontabs, the system has `/etc/crontab` and drop-in files in `/etc/cron.d/`. These have one **extra** field — the **user** to run as — between the time and the command: ``` 30 2 * * 0  root  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh ``` There are also ready-made directories `/etc/cron.hourly`, `/etc/cron.daily`, etc., where any script is run on that schedule. Who may use cron is controlled by `/etc/cron.allow` and `/etc/cron.deny`.
A **systemd timer** does the same job as cron but is integrated with systemd, so it gets logging, dependencies and better control. A timer always comes in **two files** with the same base name:
a **.service** unit that says *what* to run,
a **.timer** unit that says *when* to run it.
The timer starts its matching service. Put both in `/etc/systemd/system/`.
The `.timer` file's key line is `OnCalendar=`, which uses the format `DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second`:
`OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00` runs every day at 02:00. Shortcuts like `daily`, `weekly`, `hourly` also work.
`OnBootSec=15min` runs 15 minutes after boot; pair it with `OnUnitActiveSec=1h` to then repeat every hour.
`Persistent=true` means if the machine was **off** at the scheduled time, the job runs soon after the next boot (like anacron).
The `[Install]` section should say `WantedBy=timers.target`, and you enable the **timer** (not the service): `systemctl enable --now backup.timer`.
`systemctl list-timers` shows all timers with their next and last run times.
`systemd-analyze calendar "Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00"` checks what a calendar expression means and when it fires next — great for testing before you commit.
After creating or editing any unit file, run `systemctl daemon-reload` so systemd re-reads it.

systemd can also create and clean up temporary files/directories using rules in `/etc/tmpfiles.d/*.conf`. A rule like `d /run/myapp 0755 root root 1d` means "create this directory at boot and delete files in it older than 1 day". Apply now with `systemd-tmpfiles --create` and clean with `systemd-tmpfiles --clean`.

Different workloads want different settings — a laptop wants power saving, a database server wants throughput. The **tuned** service bundles these into **profiles** so you can switch with one command:
`tuned-adm active` shows the current profile.
`tuned-adm list` lists all available profiles.
`tuned-adm recommend` suggests the best profile for this machine (on a VM it usually recommends `virtual-guest`).
`tuned-adm profile virtual-guest` applies a profile; the choice persists while the tuned service is enabled.
Make sure the service runs: `systemctl enable --now tuned`.

Every process has a **nice value** from **−20** (highest priority, takes the most CPU) to **19** (lowest, most generous to others). The default is 0. A "nicer" process (higher number) yields CPU to others.
`nice -n 10 command` starts a command with nice value +10.
`renice -n 5 -p 1234` changes running PID 1234 to nice value 5.
Only **root** can lower a nice value (give higher priority / a negative number); a normal user can only raise their own processes' nice value.
The nice value shows in the **NI** column of `top` and `ps -o pid,ni,comm`.

For controlled tests you can bind a process to specific CPUs with `taskset -c 0 command`. Combined with nice, this shows clearly how priority affects CPU sharing when two processes compete on the same core.

27.h: What SELinux is and why it exists

blocks.x: Standard permissions (rwx) are **discretionary** — the file owner decides access. **SELinux** (Security-Enhanced Linux) adds a second, **mandatory** layer that the system enforces regardless of the owner. Even if a service is tricked into misbehaving, SELinux policy limits what it can touch. It is a major reason RHEL is considered secure, and the exam expects you to keep it **enforcing** and fix problems, not switch it off.
SELinux has three modes:
**Enforcing** — policy is applied and violations are blocked (and logged).
**Permissive** — policy is **not** enforced, but violations are still **logged**. Useful for troubleshooting.
**Disabled** — off entirely (avoid on the exam).

Check the mode with `getenforce` or the fuller `sestatus`. Switch temporarily with `setenforce 0` (permissive) or `setenforce 1` (enforcing) — but note `setenforce` can only toggle between enforcing and permissive, not fully disable. The **permanent** setting lives in `/etc/selinux/config` (the `SELINUX=` line); fully disabling requires a reboot.

Every file and process carries an SELinux **context** of the form `user:role:type:level`, for example `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`. In the everyday "targeted" policy, the part that matters most is the **type** (ending in `_t`). Policy rules say which process types may access which file types — e.g. the web server runs as `httpd_t` and is only allowed to read files labelled `httpd_sys_content_t`.
`ls -Z file` shows a file's context; `ps -eZ | grep httpd` shows process contexts; `id -Z` shows your own.

This is the classic beginner trap: when you **move** a file with `mv`, it **keeps its original context**, which may be wrong for its new location — so a service is denied access. **Copying** (`cp`) usually gives the destination's default context. The correct fix is to relabel to the policy default with `restorecon` (covered next day). A denial in permissive mode is allowed but logged, which is exactly how you diagnose these problems safely.
When a file has the wrong SELinux type, you need to relabel it — and make that relabel **stick** even after a full filesystem relabel. There are two tools, and using the right one matters:
`chcon -t type file` changes the label **now**, but it is **temporary** — a relabel or `restorecon` will revert it. Avoid it for anything permanent.

`semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/web(/.*)?'` **records** a rule in the policy so the path always gets that type. The `(/.*)?` is a regular expression meaning "this directory and everything under it".

`restorecon -Rv /web` then **applies** the recorded rules to the files, setting each to its correct type (`-R` recursive, `-v` verbose). The exam answer is almost always **semanage fcontext + restorecon**, never chcon.
Some policy behaviour is optional and controlled by **booleans** — named on/off switches. For example `httpd_enable_homedirs` lets the web server read users' home directories.
`getsebool -a | grep httpd` lists httpd-related booleans and their state; `semanage boolean -l` adds a description.
`setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on` turns one **on permanently** (the `-P` writes it to disk; without `-P` the change is lost at reboot).
`semanage boolean -l -C` shows only the booleans you have changed from their defaults.
SELinux also controls which **ports** a service may use. If you make a service listen on a non-standard port, SELinux will block the bind until the port is labelled correctly:
`semanage port -l | grep http` shows which ports carry the `http_port_t` type (80, 443, 8008, 8009, 8443 by default).
`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888` **adds** port 8888 as an http port. If the port already has another type, use `-m` (modify) instead of `-a`.
The `semanage` command comes from the **policycoreutils-python-utils** package — install it if `semanage` is missing.

When something is blocked, the reason is logged as an **AVC denial** in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. Search recent ones with `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent`, and get a plain-language explanation and suggested fix with `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log` (from the setroubleshoot-server package). A methodical order — check the file context, the port label, then the relevant boolean — solves the large majority of SELinux problems without ever disabling it.

A physical disk (like `/dev/vdb`) is usually divided into **partitions** (`/dev/vdb1`, `/dev/vdb2`). A **partition table** at the start of the disk records where each partition begins and ends. Modern systems use the **GPT** (GUID Partition Table) format, which replaced the old MBR and supports large disks and many partitions.
`lsblk` shows disks and partitions as a tree — always start here to see the layout.
`parted` edits partition tables. Two commands you must know:
`parted /dev/vdb mklabel gpt` writes a **new, empty** GPT table. **Warning:** this erases every existing partition — only run it on a blank disk.

`parted /dev/vdb mkpart data xfs 1MiB 1025MiB` creates a partition. On GPT the first argument is a **name**, then a filesystem hint, then the start and end. Always use **MiB** units and start the first partition at 1MiB so it is properly **aligned** and leaves room for the GPT header.
`parted /dev/vdb print` shows the table; add `unit MiB print free` to see free space so you know where to start the next one.
After creating a partition, run `udevadm settle` so the device file (`/dev/vdb1`) appears before you format it.
Creating a partition does not make it usable — you must put a **filesystem** on it and mount it:
`mkfs.xfs /dev/vdb1` formats it as XFS (RHEL's default). `blkid /dev/vdb1` then shows its **UUID**.
`mount /dev/vdb1 /mnt/data` mounts it for now.

For a mount to survive reboots, add a line to `/etc/fstab` with **six fields**: ``` device        mountpoint   type   options    dump  fsck UUID=1b2c...  /mnt/data    xfs    defaults   0     0 ``` Use `UUID=` (or `LABEL=`) rather than `/dev/vdb1`, because device names can change between boots but the UUID does not. After editing fstab, **always test** with `systemctl daemon-reload` then `mount -a` (which mounts everything not yet mounted) before you reboot — a broken fstab line drops the boot into emergency mode. Run `findmnt --verify` for a deeper check.

**Swap** is disk space the kernel uses as overflow when physical RAM fills up — inactive memory pages are moved to swap so RAM is freed for active work. It is not a replacement for RAM, but it prevents out-of-memory crashes. Swap can live on a **partition**, a **logical volume**, or a **file**.
The process mirrors making a filesystem, but with swap-specific tools:
Create the partition with a swap hint: `parted /dev/vdb mkpart swap1 linux-swap 1025MiB 1537MiB`, then `udevadm settle`.
`mkswap /dev/vdb2` initialises it as swap (and prints a new UUID).
`swapon /dev/vdb2` turns it on now; `swapoff /dev/vdb2` turns it off.

Add a line to `/etc/fstab` — the mount-point field is `none` (or `swap`) and the type is `swap`: ``` UUID=<uuid>  none  swap  defaults  0 0 ``` Test it without rebooting using `swapon -a` (which activates all swap listed in fstab); `mount -a` ignores swap entries, so this separate step matters.
`swapon --show` (or `swapon -s`, or `cat /proc/swaps`) lists active swap areas; `free -h` shows total swap alongside RAM.
If you have several swap areas, give one priority with the `pri=N` option in fstab (higher numbers are used first): `UUID=... none swap pri=10 0 0`.
"Add swap non-destructively" — a common exam phrase — means add new swap using free space **without** deleting or disturbing existing partitions or swap.
Plain partitions are rigid — resizing them is awkward. **LVM** (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer so you can grow, shrink and combine storage easily. It has three levels:
**Physical Volumes (PV)** — the raw partitions or disks you hand to LVM.
**Volume Group (VG)** — a pool made by combining one or more PVs.
**Logical Volumes (LV)** — the usable "virtual partitions" you carve out of the VG, format and mount.
Space in a VG is measured in fixed chunks called **physical extents** (PE), 4 MiB by default.

31.h: Building an LVM stack step by step

blocks.x: The commands follow the three levels in order:
`pvcreate /dev/vdb1` marks a partition as a physical volume. Check with `pvs`.
`vgcreate vgdata /dev/vdb1` creates a volume group from it. Add `-s 16M` to set a custom extent size. Check with `vgs` or `vgdisplay`.

`lvcreate -n lvdata -L 500M vgdata` creates a 500 MiB logical volume named lvdata. Use `-L` for a size, or `-l 60` for a number of **extents**, or `-l 100%FREE` to use all remaining space. Check with `lvs`.
Then treat the LV like any partition: `mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvdata`, make a mount point, and add it to `/etc/fstab`.

A logical volume can be reached by two equivalent paths: `/dev/vgdata/lvdata` and `/dev/mapper/vgdata-lvdata` — both work in fstab, and because LV names are stable they are as reliable as a UUID. When a task gives extents and an extent size, size = extents × extent size (e.g. 60 extents × 16 MiB = 960 MiB). `-L` rounds up to a whole number of extents.
The short summaries are `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs`; the detailed versions are `pvdisplay`, `vgdisplay`, `lvdisplay`. `vgdisplay` shows the "PE Size" (extent size) and how many free extents remain.
The big advantage of LVM is easy resizing. Growing an LV is a **two-part** job: enlarge the LV, then enlarge the filesystem on it. The safe way does both at once:

`lvextend -r -L +200M /dev/vgdata/lvdata` grows the LV by 200 MiB **and** (thanks to `-r`, "resize filesystem") grows the filesystem to match. Without `-r` you would have to run the filesystem grow tool separately.
`-L +200M` **adds** 200 MiB; `-L 1G` **sets** the total to 1 GiB. Read the task: "grow by" is relative (`+`), "resize to" is absolute.
If you extend the LV without `-r`, `df -h` still shows the old size until you grow the filesystem:
**XFS**: `xfs_growfs /mnt/data` — note it takes the **mount point**, and XFS grows only while mounted.
**ext4**: `resize2fs /dev/vgdata/lvdata` — takes the **device**.
Important limitation: **XFS can only grow, never shrink.** ext4 can shrink (while unmounted). To make XFS smaller you must back up, recreate it smaller, and restore.

32.h: When the volume group is full

blocks.x: If the VG has no free space, you cannot grow an LV until you add capacity:
`vgextend vgdata /dev/vdc1` adds another physical volume to the group (run `pvcreate` on it first if needed).
To remove a PV, first move its data off with `pvmove /dev/vdb1`, then `vgreduce vgdata /dev/vdb1`, then `pvremove /dev/vdb1`.
To tear an LVM stack down cleanly, always work top-down: unmount, remove the fstab line, `lvremove`, `vgremove`, `pvremove`.
RHEL supports several filesystems, and the exam expects you to create and mount each:
**XFS** — RHEL's default; robust and fast; can only grow.
**ext4** — the long-standing Linux default; can grow **and** shrink.
**VFAT** — the FAT filesystem for compatibility with other systems (USB sticks, EFI). It stores **no** Linux ownership or permissions.
The tools: `mkfs.xfs` (from xfsprogs), `mkfs.ext4` (from e2fsprogs), and `mkfs.vfat` (from dosfstools). Add `-f` to overwrite an existing filesystem.
A **label** is a friendly name you can mount by, as an alternative to the UUID:
XFS: set with `xfs_admin -L DATA /dev/vdb1` (unmounted) or at creation `mkfs.xfs -L DATA`.
ext4: `e2label /dev/vdb2 BACKUP` or `tune2fs -L`.
VFAT: `fatlabel /dev/vdb5 WINDATA`, or at creation `mkfs.vfat -n WINDATA`. Note VFAT's label option is `-n`, while XFS/ext4 use `-L`.
Then mount by `LABEL=DATA` in fstab instead of the UUID.

Because VFAT has no concept of Linux ownership, you assign it at mount time with options: `mount -o uid=2000,gid=2000 /dev/vdb5 /mnt/usb`. In fstab: `UUID=1A2B-3C4D /mnt/usb vfat uid=2000,gid=2000 0 0` (VFAT UUIDs are short, like `1A2B-3C4D`).

`nofail` lets the boot continue even if that device is missing (good for removable or network disks); `noauto` means "do not mount at boot at all"; `ro`/`rw` for read-only/read-write; remount live with `mount -o remount,ro /mnt/data`.
Inspect: `xfs_info /mnt/data` for XFS geometry; `tune2fs -l /dev/...` for ext4; `findmnt -o TARGET,OPTIONS /mnt/data` to see how something is mounted.

**NFS** (Network File System) lets a server **share** (export) a directory over the network so client machines can **mount** it and use it as if it were local. It is the standard way to share files between Linux systems. The client tools come from the **nfs-utils** package.

34.h: Mounting an NFS share on the client

blocks.x: `mount -t nfs node2:/shares/docs /mnt/docs` mounts the export now (the mount point must exist). The syntax is `server:/exported/path`.
`showmount -e node2` lists what a server exports (needs the server's supporting services reachable).
RHEL defaults to **NFSv4**; force a version with `-o nfsvers=4.2` or `-o vers=3` if a task asks.
`findmnt -t nfs4` shows mounted NFS filesystems and their options.

Add it to `/etc/fstab` with the type `nfs` and the `_netdev` option (which tells the system to wait for the network before mounting): ``` node2:/shares/docs  /mnt/docs  nfs  defaults,_netdev  0 0 ``` The dump and fsck fields are `0 0` because there is nothing local to check. Test with `mount -a` and confirm with `findmnt /mnt/docs`.

On the server, exports are defined in `/etc/exports`, one line each: `/shares/docs 192.168.122.0/24(rw,sync)`. Apply changes with `exportfs -rv`, run the `nfs-server` service, and open the firewall for the `nfs` service (plus `rpc-bind` and `mountd` if clients use `showmount`). Understanding the server helps you troubleshoot a failing client mount — a hang usually means a firewall or export problem.

Mounting every network share in `/etc/fstab` means they are all mounted at boot and stay mounted, even when unused. **autofs** mounts a share **on demand** — only when someone accesses it — and unmounts it automatically after a period of inactivity. This is ideal for home directories and shares that are not always needed. It is provided by the **autofs** package and service.

35.h: The master map and the mount maps

blocks.x: autofs configuration has two layers:
The **master map** entries live in files under `/etc/auto.master.d/` ending in `.autofs`. Each line links a **base directory** to a **mount map** file, e.g. `/shares  /etc/auto.shares`.

The **mount map** (e.g. `/etc/auto.shares`) lists the actual mounts: `work  -rw,sync  node2:/shares/work`. Here `work` becomes a subdirectory of the base directory, so this mounts at `/shares/work` the first time it is accessed.
You do **not** create the subdirectories yourself — autofs manages the base directory entirely. Enable it with `systemctl enable --now autofs`; after editing maps, `systemctl reload autofs`.
The example above is an **indirect map**: keys become subdirectories under one base. `ls /shares` shows nothing until you actually access `/shares/work`.
A **direct map** uses `/-` as the base in the master map, and each key is a full path: `/mnt/docs  -ro  node2:/shares/docs`.

A **wildcard map** uses `*` and `&` to serve any key automatically — perfect for home directories: `*  -rw,sync  node2:/rhome/&` mounts `node2:/rhome/<name>` whenever `/rhome/<name>` is accessed. The `&` is replaced by whatever key was requested.

A very common exam task combines a user with no local home and an autofs wildcard map, so the user's home is fetched from an NFS server on login. Create the user with `useradd -M` (no local home) and a matching home path, add the master and wildcard map entries, and confirm with `su - user` (which triggers the mount) and `findmnt`.
systemd groups the system into **targets** — named states that pull in a set of services. A target is roughly the modern replacement for old "runlevels". The two you care about most:
**multi-user.target** — a full multi-user system with networking, but **no graphical desktop** (text login).
**graphical.target** — everything in multi-user plus the desktop.
Special targets help with repair: **rescue.target** (single-user, root shell, local filesystems mounted) and **emergency.target** (the most minimal — only the root filesystem, mounted read-only).

36.h: Viewing and setting the default target

blocks.x: `systemctl get-default` shows which target the system boots into.
`systemctl set-default multi-user.target` changes it permanently (this just re-points the `/etc/systemd/system/default.target` symlink).
`systemctl isolate multi-user.target` switches to a target **right now** without rebooting, stopping anything not needed by it (run it from the console, since switching can stop your SSH session).

To enter a target for a **single** boot (say, to repair something), interrupt the boot loader: at the GRUB menu press **e** to edit, find the line starting with `linux`, add `systemd.unit=rescue.target` at the end, and press **Ctrl+X** to boot. The change applies only to that boot.

Knowing the order tells you where to intervene when boot fails: 1. **Firmware (BIOS/UEFI)** powers on and finds the boot device. 2. **GRUB2** (the boot loader) loads and shows its menu. 3. The **kernel and initramfs** load and mount the real root filesystem. 4. **systemd** (PID 1) starts and brings the system up to the default target.

If you don't know the root password, you regain access by interrupting the boot into the initramfs, before the real system takes over. This is a signature RHCSA task, and the steps are worth memorising:
Reboot and at the GRUB menu press **e**. On the line starting with `linux`, add **`rd.break`** at the end, then **Ctrl+X**.
You land in a tiny emergency shell where the real root filesystem is mounted **read-only** at `/sysroot`.
`mount -o remount,rw /sysroot` — remount it writable.
`chroot /sysroot` — make `/sysroot` act as `/` so paths like `/etc/shadow` are the real ones.
`passwd root` — set the new password.
`touch /.autorelabel` — **crucial**: the changed `/etc/shadow` needs the correct SELinux label, and this flag makes the next boot relabel the filesystem. Skipping it can lock everyone out.
`exit`, then `exit` again — the system relabels (this takes a few minutes) and reboots. Log in with the new password.
A bad line in `/etc/fstab` (a wrong UUID, a missing device) stops the boot and drops you into **emergency mode**, asking for the root password. To fix it:
Enter the root password. The root filesystem is mounted **read-only**, so run `mount -o remount,rw /` first.
Edit `/etc/fstab` to correct or comment out the bad line (check real UUIDs with `blkid`).
`systemctl daemon-reload` then `mount -a` to test the fix before rebooting.
The lesson: after **every** fstab change, test with `mount -a` immediately — never discover the mistake at the next reboot.

For a device that may not always be present (a removable disk, an NFS share), add the **`nofail`** mount option in fstab. Then, if the device is missing at boot, the system logs it and continues instead of dropping into emergency mode.

**GRUB2** is the boot loader — the program that runs after the firmware, shows the menu of installed kernels, and loads the one you choose. Being able to edit its settings and kernel options is a required skill.

38.h: Editing kernel options safely with grubby

blocks.x: Rather than hand-editing generated files, use `grubby` to manage kernel entries and their command-line options:
`grubby --default-kernel` shows which kernel boots by default; `grubby --info=ALL` lists every entry with its options.
`grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="console=ttyS0"` adds a kernel argument to **all** kernels; use `--update-kernel=DEFAULT` to affect only the default one.
`grubby --remove-args="quiet"` removes an argument.
`grubby --set-default /boot/vmlinuz-<version>` makes a specific kernel the default.

Changes take effect at the next boot; confirm with `cat /proc/cmdline` afterward. The individual menu entries live in `/boot/loader/entries/*.conf` (Boot Loader Specification files), which grubby edits for you.
Global settings like the menu timeout live in `/etc/default/grub` (e.g. `GRUB_TIMEOUT=10`). This file is a **source**, not the live config — after editing it you must regenerate the real config:
`grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` rebuilds it (this path is correct for both BIOS and UEFI on RHEL 9/10).

For a temporary change (testing), don't edit files at all — at the GRUB menu press **e**, add the option to the `linux` line, and press **Ctrl+X**. It applies to that boot only and is forgotten afterward.

**firewalld** is RHEL's firewall management service. It decides which incoming network connections are allowed. You manage it with the `firewall-cmd` command, and it organises rules into **zones** — each zone is a trust level (public, trusted, drop, internal, dmz…) that can be attached to network interfaces or source addresses.

39.h: The permanent vs runtime rule (the #1 gotcha)

blocks.x: firewalld keeps two rule sets: the **runtime** rules (active now, lost at reboot) and the **permanent** rules (saved to disk, loaded at boot). This trips up everyone:
`firewall-cmd --add-service=http` changes only the **runtime** — gone after reboot.
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http` saves it **permanently** but does **not** apply it now.

The reliable pattern is: add with `--permanent`, then `firewall-cmd --reload` to make the permanent rules active immediately. `firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent` saves current runtime rules as permanent if you tested them live.
Allow a named service: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http` (a service is a predefined set of ports; see `firewall-cmd --get-services`, defined in `/usr/lib/firewalld/services/*.xml`).
Open a specific port: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp`.
Remove: `--remove-service=` / `--remove-port=`.
Inspect: `firewall-cmd --list-all` (current zone), `--list-all-zones` (all), `--get-default-zone`, `--get-active-zones`.
Put a source address into a zone: `firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=192.168.122.12` gives that host full access.

For finer control, a **rich rule** combines source, service, action and logging: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.50.0/24" service name="ssh" reject'` refuses SSH from one subnet. Note **reject** replies "refused" while **drop** silently discards. `man firewalld.richlanguage` has copyable examples.

40.h: Security is layered — check all three

blocks.x: When a network service does not work, three separate layers can be blocking it, and a real administrator checks each in order: 1. **The service itself** — is it running, and listening on the right port? (`systemctl status`, `ss -tulpn`). 2. **SELinux** — is the port labelled and are the file contexts correct? A "Permission denied" when a service tries to **bind** to a new port is usually SELinux, not the firewall. 3. **The firewall** — is the port open to other machines? A service that works with `curl localhost` but not from another host points to the firewall. The firewall never stops a *local* service from starting; it only blocks *incoming* traffic. Keep this mental model and you will fix problems methodically instead of guessing.

40.h: Running a service on a non-standard port

blocks.x: Putting, say, a web server on port 8888 needs all three layers aligned:
Configure the service to listen on 8888 (edit its config).
Tell SELinux the port is allowed: `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`.
Open the firewall: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8888/tcp && firewall-cmd --reload`.
Restart the service. Then test with `curl http://host:8888/` from another machine.

40.h: SSH on an extra port and diagnosing

blocks.x: The same pattern applies to running sshd on an additional port: add `Port 2222` to the sshd config, label it with `semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222`, open `2222/tcp` in the firewall, and restart sshd. To diagnose, `ss -tlnp | grep 2222` confirms something is listening, and a capture with `tcpdump` shows whether a connection gets no reply (blocked) versus a reset (refused). The golden rule: fix contexts, ports and firewall rules — never "fix" a problem by turning SELinux or the firewall off.

A **snapshot** captures a logical volume at a moment in time so you can roll back to it later. It is clever about space: it uses **copy-on-write**, meaning it starts almost empty and only stores the **original** version of blocks that change on the source volume afterward. So a snapshot begins tiny and grows as the origin is modified.
`lvcreate -s -n datasnap -L 1G /dev/vgdata/lvdata` creates a 1 GiB snapshot of lvdata (`-s` = snapshot; the origin is the last argument).
`lvs -a -o +origin,data_percent` shows snapshots with their **Origin** and **Data%** columns. Watch Data% closely.
**If a snapshot fills to 100%, it becomes invalid and is dropped** — so size it for the amount of change you expect during its life. (lvm.conf can enable auto-extend.)
To restore the origin to the snapshot's state, **merge** the snapshot back:

`lvconvert --merge /dev/vgdata/datasnap`. If the origin is currently in use, the merge completes at the next activation/reboot; after merging, the snapshot is removed automatically. Unmount the origin first for an immediate merge.

A common professional use is taking a **consistent backup**: snapshot the volume (freezing a moment), mount the snapshot read-only, back it up with tar while the real volume keeps changing, then remove the snapshot. Remember snapshots are a fast local "undo", **not** a substitute for real off-machine backups.

Normally an LV reserves its full size up front. **Thin provisioning** lets logical volumes share a common **thin pool** and consume space only as they actually write data — so you can present more logical space than physically exists (over-provisioning):
`lvcreate --type thin-pool -L 1G -n tpool vgdata` creates the pool.
`lvcreate -V 5G -T vgdata/tpool -n tvol` creates a thin volume whose **virtual** size (5 G) exceeds the pool (1 G).
The risk: if the **pool** fills, writes to any thin volume fail. Watch the pool's Data% and Meta% with `lvs`, and extend the **pool** in time with `lvextend -L +1G vgdata/tpool`.
A **striped** LV spreads data across several physical volumes so reads and writes happen in parallel — faster I/O, but **no redundancy** (losing one PV loses the volume):
`lvcreate --type striped -i 2 -I 64 -L 1G -n fast vgdata` uses `-i` stripes across 2 PVs with a `-I` 64 KiB stripe size.
LVM can build RAID levels directly:
`raid1` (`lvcreate --type raid1 -m 1 -L 500M -n safe vgdata`) mirrors data across two legs and survives one device failing (`-m 1` = one mirror copy).
`raid5` (`--type raid5 -i 3`) stripes with parity across at least 3 devices and tolerates one failure.
Inspect the underlying devices and sync state with `lvs -a -o +devices,segtype,sync_percent`.

**Stratis** is a newer local storage manager that layers on top of LVM and device-mapper to give you pools and thin XFS filesystems with simple commands, without managing PVs/VGs/LVs by hand. Manage it with the `stratis` command and the `stratisd` service:
`stratis pool create mypool /dev/vdb` builds a pool; `stratis pool add-data mypool /dev/vdc` grows it live.
`stratis filesystem create mypool data` makes a filesystem at `/dev/stratis/mypool/data`.
Because the device is not ready until `stratisd` runs, its `/etc/fstab` line needs the option `x-systemd.requires=stratisd.service` so the mount waits for the service.
