**LVM-VDO** stores data with inline **deduplication** (identical blocks stored once) and **compression**, so a volume can hold far more logical data than its physical size — ideal for backups and VM images with lots of repetition:
`lvcreate --type vdo -n vdolv -L 10G -V 30G vgdata` creates a VDO volume; check savings with `lvs -o+vdo_used_size,data_percent`.
LVM automatically backs up each volume group's metadata to `/etc/lvm/backup` (current) and `/etc/lvm/archive` (historical). If you damage a VG — say you delete an LV by mistake — you can restore it:
`vgcfgbackup vgdata` writes current metadata to a file.
`vgcfgrestore -f /etc/lvm/archive/vgdata_XXXX.vg vgdata` restores from an archive (then reactivate with `vgchange -ay vgdata`).
To physically move a VG's disks to another machine, deactivate its LVs and use `vgexport`, then `vgimport` on the new host.
When SELinux blocks something in enforcing mode, it records an **AVC** (Access Vector Cache) denial in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. Reading and understanding these is the core troubleshooting skill:
`ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` searches for recent denials (`-m AVC` filters the message type, `-ts recent` the time window).
Pipe a denial to `audit2why` for a plain-language explanation of **why** it happened — often pointing at a boolean or a wrong context.
If no boolean or correct label fixes a legitimate denial, you can generate a small custom policy **module** that permits exactly those actions:
`audit2allow -a -M mymodule` reads the denials and produces `mymodule.pp` (always review the human-readable `mymodule.te` it also writes).
`semodule -i mymodule.pp` loads it; `semodule -l` lists loaded modules; `semodule -r mymodule` removes it.
This is a **last resort** — always try labels and booleans first, because they are the intended fix.

54.h: Guided fixes and targeted permissive mode

blocks.x: `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log` (from setroubleshoot-server) analyses denials and prints suggested commands.

`semanage permissive -a httpd_t` puts a **single** domain (here the web server) into permissive mode so you can collect all its denials while the rest of the system stays enforcing — much safer than `setenforce 0`. Remove it afterward with `semanage permissive -d httpd_t`.

54.h: The right order to fix a denial

blocks.x: For a real problem, work through: (1) is the **file context** correct? fix with `restorecon`; (2) is a **boolean** needed? set it; (3) is a **port** label needed? add it. Only if none of those apply do you build a custom module. Fixing labels — never disabling SELinux — is always the exam-correct answer.

55.h: chcon vs semanage fcontext (again, because it matters)

blocks.x: This distinction is the heart of SELinux file management:
`chcon -t type file` changes a label **now** but does not survive a relabel — temporary.
`semanage fcontext -a -t type 'regex'` records a **permanent** rule in policy; `restorecon -Rv path` then applies it. Always prefer semanage + restorecon.
File-context rules use regular expressions; `'/web(/.*)?'` covers the directory `/web` and everything under it.
To let a service use a non-default port, add the port to the correct type:
`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888` (use `-m` to modify a port that already has a different type).
`semanage port -l | grep http` lists the ports a type already covers; `semanage port -l -C` shows only your changes.
Booleans switch optional policy behaviour on and off without editing policy:

`getsebool -a | grep httpd` lists them; `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on` enables one permanently (`-P` = persistent). Common ones let the web server reach the network or read home directories.
`semanage boolean -l -C` reviews only the ones you changed.
SELinux can also limit what a **login** may do, beyond normal permissions, by mapping Linux users to SELinux users (`user_u`, `staff_u`, `sysadm_u`):

`semanage login -a -s staff_u operator` maps the Linux user `operator` to the `staff_u` SELinux user; `semanage login -l` shows the mappings. A user mapped to `user_u`, for example, is confined even if they gain root-like tools. Check a logged-in user's context with `id -Z`.

A recap that catches everyone: **moving** a file with `mv` preserves its **old** context, so a service may be denied; **copying** picks up the destination's default. The universal fix is `restorecon -Rv /path`, which sets each file to the type the policy defines — persistent and correct, unlike a manual `chcon`.
`matchpathcon /web/index.html` (or `restorecon -n -v` for a dry run) shows the **expected** label so you can spot a mismatch against `ls -Z`.
After widespread context damage (or a password reset), you can trigger a **full relabel** on the next boot:
`touch /.autorelabel` then reboot — the system relabels everything and removes the flag. It can take a few minutes.
`restorecon -Rnv /var/www` is a safe **dry run** that lists what would change without changing anything; drop the `-n` to apply.
Container isolation is reinforced by SELinux. When you mount a host directory into a container you must relabel it so the container process (type `container_t`) may access it:

`podman run -v /srv/data:/data:Z ...` — the **:Z** relabels the host directory with a **private** container context (`container_file_t`) for that one container; lowercase **:z** labels it **shared** among containers.

For a permanent host label, use `semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t '/srv/data(/.*)?'` and `restorecon`. This layering — namespaces plus SELinux — is why rootless containers on RHEL are considered well isolated.

A **container** is a lightweight, isolated package that holds an application plus everything it needs to run, sharing the host's kernel instead of running a whole separate operating system like a virtual machine. This makes containers fast to start and small. On RHEL the tool is **Podman**, which is **daemonless** (no background service like Docker needs) and can run **rootless** (as an ordinary user) — both reasons the RHCSA favours it. Most Docker commands work identically with `podman`.

An **image** is the read-only template; a **container** is a running instance of an image. Images come from **registries** (online image stores). A full image name is `registry/namespace/name:tag`, e.g. `registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi:latest`, where the **tag** is the version.
`podman search ubi9` searches the configured registries. Which registries are searched for a bare name is set in `/etc/containers/registries.conf` (the `unqualified-search-registries` list).
`podman pull registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi` downloads an image; `podman images` lists what you have stored locally. Rootless images live under `~/.local/share/containers/storage`.
`podman login registry.redhat.io` authenticates to a registry that needs credentials.
**skopeo** works on remote images without pulling them — perfect for checking before you download:
`skopeo inspect docker://registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi` shows an image's metadata (layers, labels, digest).
`skopeo copy` can copy images between registries and local storage.
The core command is `podman run`:

`podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx` runs nginx in the background (`-d` detached), names it `web`, and maps host port 8080 to the container's port 80 (`-p host:container`). Reach it at `http://host:8080`.
`podman run --rm image cmd` runs a one-off command and removes the container when it exits (`--rm`).
`podman run -it --name shell image bash` runs **interactively** (`-i` keep input open, `-t` give a terminal) — you get a shell inside the container. It stops when you exit.
`-e VAR=value` sets an environment variable inside the container.
`podman ps` shows **running** containers; `podman ps -a` includes **stopped** ones.
`podman stop web` / `podman start web` / `podman restart web` control a container.
`podman rm web` removes a stopped container (`podman rm -f web` stops and removes in one step). A stopped container keeps existing — and using space — until you remove it.
`podman logs web` shows its output (`-f` to follow live) — the first place to look when a container misbehaves.
`podman exec -it web bash` opens a shell **inside** an already-running container to look around.
`podman inspect web` prints detailed JSON; filter one field with `--format '{{.State.Status}}'`.

A container has a writable layer, but it is **ephemeral** — remove the container and anything written inside is gone. To keep data you must store it **outside** the container using a volume. There are two kinds:
A **bind mount** maps a specific host directory in: `-v /srv/web:/usr/share/nginx/html`.
A **named volume** is Podman-managed storage: `podman volume create appdata`, then `-v appdata:/data`. List with `podman volume ls`.
On an SELinux-enforcing host (the default), a container is **denied** access to host files unless they carry a container label. Add a suffix to the volume:
`:Z` relabels the host directory with a **private** context (`container_file_t`) for that one container.
`:z` labels it **shared** among containers.

So `-v /srv/web:/usr/share/nginx/html:Z` is what makes a bind mount actually work. Without it you will see a 403/permission error and an AVC denial. For a permanent host label, use `semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t '/srv/web(/.*)?'` and `restorecon`.

Applications are often configured through environment variables. Pass them at run time with `-e NAME=value` (repeat for several), and confirm inside with `podman exec name printenv NAME` or `podman inspect name --format '{{.Config.Env}}'`.

60.h: Building your own image from a Containerfile

blocks.x: A **Containerfile** (same format as a Dockerfile) is a recipe of instructions that build a custom image. The common instructions:
**FROM** — the base image to build on (always first): `FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi`.
**RUN** — run a command **during the build**, creating a new layer: `RUN dnf install -y httpd && dnf clean all`.
**COPY** — copy files from your build directory into the image: `COPY index.html /var/www/html/index.html`.
**ENV** — set an environment variable baked into the image.
**EXPOSE** — document the port the app listens on.
**CMD** / **ENTRYPOINT** — what runs when the container **starts**. ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that are easy to override.

60.h: RUN vs CMD — build time vs run time

blocks.x: The key distinction: **RUN** happens while the image is being **built** (installing software); **CMD/ENTRYPOINT** happens when a container **starts** from the finished image. Mixing these up is the usual beginner error.
`podman build -t webapp:1.0 .` builds an image tagged `webapp:1.0` from the Containerfile in the current directory (the trailing `.` is the build context).
`podman history webapp:1.0` shows the layers each instruction created.
`podman tag webapp:1.0 webapp:latest` adds another tag; `podman save -o webapp.tar webapp:1.0` exports the image to a file.

61.h: Running a container as a systemd service

blocks.x: For a container that should start automatically at boot and be managed like any service, integrate it with systemd. On RHEL 10 the modern method is **Quadlet**: you write a small `.container` unit and systemd generates the service for you.
Put the file in `~/.config/containers/systemd/` (rootless) or `/etc/containers/systemd/` (rootful).
A minimal `webapp.container`:

``` [Container] Image=docker.io/library/nginx:latest PublishPort=8080:80 [Install] WantedBy=default.target ``` Key `[Container]` keys: `Image=`, `PublishPort=host:container`, `Volume=/host:/ctr:Z`, `Environment=`.
A Quadlet file named `webapp.container` produces a service called `webapp.service`:
After creating or editing the unit, `systemctl --user daemon-reload` (rootless) regenerates the service.
`systemctl --user start webapp.service` starts it; check with `systemctl --user status webapp.service`.
By default, a rootless user's services stop when their last login session ends. To make them run at boot and keep running after logout, enable **lingering**:
`loginctl enable-linger $USER`. Confirm with `loginctl show-user $USER | grep Linger`.

On RHEL 9 you may still see `podman generate systemd --new --name web --files`, which writes a systemd unit for an existing container; you copy it to `~/.config/systemd/user/` and `systemctl --user enable --now` it. Quadlet is the current, preferred approach, but recognise both.
A **pod** groups several containers that share networking — the same idea as a Kubernetes pod. Containers in a pod reach each other on `localhost` and share the pod's published ports:
`podman pod create --name webpod -p 8080:80` creates a pod; `podman run -d --pod webpod --name web nginx` adds a container to it; `podman pod ps` lists pods.
`podman stats` shows live CPU/memory/I/O per container (`--no-stream` for one snapshot).
`podman cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf` copies files out of (or into) a container, like `docker cp`.
`podman system df` shows space used; `podman container prune` removes stopped containers and `podman image prune -a` removes unused images to reclaim space.
`podman auto-update` checks the registry and restarts a labelled container if a newer image exists (pairs with a systemd timer).
When a container keeps exiting, the method is simple and reliable:
`podman ps -a` shows its exit code; `podman logs <name>` almost always reveals the cause (a bad command, a missing file, a permission problem).
`podman inspect <name> --format '{{...}}'` extracts specific details (IP address, state).
Resist the urge to reboot the host or disable SELinux — read the logs, fix the real cause (often a volume label or a wrong command), and re-run.

NetworkManager separates the **device** (the network card, e.g. `eth0`) from the **connection profile** (a saved configuration). One device can have several profiles; you activate whichever you need. On RHEL 9/10, profiles are stored as **keyfiles** in `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/` ending in `.nmconnection`. After hand-editing a keyfile, run `nmcli con reload`.
Many settings are **lists** (addresses, DNS servers, routes). nmcli lets you add or remove single items without replacing the whole list:
`nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.addresses 10.0.0.5/24` **appends** a second address.
`nmcli con mod eth0 -ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8` removes one DNS entry.
No prefix replaces the entire list.
Changes only take effect when you re-activate the profile: `nmcli con up eth0`.
Add a persistent route with `nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.routes "192.168.50.0/24 192.168.1.254"` (reach that subnet via that gateway). This survives reboots, unlike a bare `ip route add`.
On a host with two uplinks, `ipv4.route-metric` sets which is preferred — **lower wins**. Set a lower metric on the primary connection so its default route is chosen.
`nmcli con mod eth0 connection.autoconnect yes` makes a profile come up at boot.
`nmcli -f ipv4 con show eth0` shows all IPv4 settings of a profile; `nmcli dev show eth0 | grep -i dns` shows the DNS it applies.

**Bonding** combines two or more network cards into one logical interface (`bond0`) for **redundancy** (survive a cable/switch failure) or **more bandwidth**. On RHEL 9/10 use bonding — the older "teaming" (teamd) was removed. The member interfaces are called **ports**, and the bond that controls them is the **controller**.
The bonding **mode** decides how the ports are used:
**active-backup (mode 1)** — one port is active at a time; if it fails, another takes over. Needs **no** special switch configuration — the safe default for redundancy.
**802.3ad (mode 4, LACP)** — aggregates ports for throughput, but the switch must be configured for it.
**balance-rr (mode 0)** — round-robin across ports.
The `miimon` option sets how often (in milliseconds) the link is checked for failover, e.g. `miimon=100`.
Create the bond: `nmcli con add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 bond.options "mode=active-backup,miimon=100"` (add `ipv4.addresses`/`ipv4.method manual` for a static IP).
Add each NIC as a port: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name bond0-p1 ifname eth1 master bond0` (repeat for eth2). Ports have no IP of their own.
Bring it up with `nmcli con up bond0`.
`cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0` shows the mode, each port's link state, and which port is currently active.
To test failover, bring the active port down (`nmcli con down bond0-p1`) and confirm the bond switches to the other while connectivity continues (`ping`).

firewalld organises rules into **zones**, each a trust level bound to interfaces or source addresses. `public` is the cautious default; `trusted` allows everything; `drop` silently discards. `firewall-cmd --get-active-zones` shows which interfaces/sources map to which zone, and `--set-default-zone=` changes the default.
When a host **routes** traffic for a private network out to the internet, it must translate the private source addresses to its own — this is **masquerading** (source NAT):
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-masquerade` enables it. It is required whenever the host acts as a gateway/router for other machines.
firewalld can redirect traffic arriving on one port to another port (or host):
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080` sends incoming port 80 to a service on 8080. Forwarding to another **host** also needs masquerade.
For precise control — matching a specific source, logging, rate-limiting — use a **rich rule**:
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.66" log prefix="DROP66 " level="info" drop'` logs and drops traffic from one host.
Remember **reject** replies "refused" while **drop** stays silent (the host appears offline). Always follow permanent changes with `firewall-cmd --reload`.

**nftables** is the modern Linux packet-filtering framework that replaced the old iptables. Importantly, **firewalld uses nftables as its backend** — so on a normal RHEL system you manage the firewall through firewalld, and nftables is what actually enforces the rules underneath. You would write raw nftables rules only on a host **not** using firewalld; mixing the two on one host causes conflicts.
nftables is organised in three levels:
A **table** (with a **family** such as `inet` for both IPv4+IPv6) holds chains.
A **chain** holds rules. A **base chain** must declare a **type**, a **hook** (input/forward/output) and a **priority**, plus a default **policy** (accept or drop).
**Rules** match traffic and take an action.
Example base chain: `type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;`.
`nft list ruleset` shows the entire active ruleset (with firewalld running, you see firewalld's generated tables here).

Build one by hand: `nft add table inet filter`, then `nft add chain inet filter input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }'`, then rules like `nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept` and `nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept`.
`nft -a list table inet filter` shows rule **handles**; delete one with `nft delete rule inet filter input handle N`.
To load a ruleset at boot, save it to `/etc/nftables.conf` (starting with `#!/usr/sbin/nft -f` and `flush ruleset`) and enable the `nftables` service: `systemctl enable --now nftables`.
A **bridge** (`br0`) acts like a virtual switch in software, most commonly used to connect **virtual machines** to the physical network so they appear on the LAN directly. Build one with nmcli:

`nmcli con add type bridge con-name br0 ifname br0` (add an IP as needed), then attach a NIC as a port: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name br0-port ifname eth1 master br0`. The bridge, not the NIC, then holds the IP.
A **VLAN** (Virtual LAN) lets one physical NIC carry several isolated networks, each tagged with an 802.1Q **VLAN ID**. The switch port must be a **trunk** that allows those VLANs:
`nmcli con add type vlan con-name vlan20 ifname eth0.20 dev eth0 id 20 ipv4.addresses 192.168.20.5/24 ipv4.method manual` creates VLAN 20 on eth0 (the interface name convention is `device.vlanid`).
Persist a route in a profile: `nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.routes "10.10.0.0/16 192.168.1.254"`. A bare `ip route add` is lost on reboot.

To let a host **forward** packets between networks (act as a router), enable IP forwarding persistently: put `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-forward.conf` and apply with `sysctl --system`. Combine with masquerade when routing to the internet.
**Policy routing** with `ip rule` can choose different routing tables based on the source address, for advanced multi-uplink setups.

When "I can't reach a server", resist guessing and work **up the stack** in order — each step tells you the next: 1. **Link** — is the interface up with an IP? `ip -br a`, `ip -br link`. 2. **Route** — is there a default gateway? `ip route`. 3. **Gateway** — can you reach it? `ping -c2 <gateway>`. 4. **DNS** — does the name resolve? `getent hosts <name>` or `dig <name>`. 5. **Service/port** — is the remote port open? `nc -zv host 443`. Whichever step fails tells you which layer to fix.
`ss -tulpn` lists listening TCP/UDP ports with the owning process (t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric) — the modern replacement for `netstat`.
`ip -br a` / `ip route` give a quick health check of addresses and routing.
`getent hosts name` resolves a name using the system's full order (files then DNS), reflecting exactly what applications see — better than a raw DNS query when `/etc/hosts` is involved.
`mtr` combines ping and traceroute to show per-hop loss over time; `ethtool eth0` shows link speed, duplex and whether the link is detected.
`ping` reaches an IP but a name fails → a **DNS** problem, not connectivity.
A local `curl localhost` works but another host cannot connect → the **firewall**.
A service refuses to **bind** to a new port with "Permission denied" → **SELinux** (label the port).

Watch NetworkManager's own logs during changes with `journalctl -u NetworkManager -f`, and capture a stubborn connection with `tcpdump` — a SYN with no reply means blocked, a RST means refused. Methodical layering beats random rebooting every time.
